answer.rationale: Constraints bind hard: 14 days to expiry with no auto-renew, line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, and only one decision available. That combination rules out the options that add execution risk or leave supply uncovered. Switching primary vendor (memory_c2) buys unit cost but that record explicitly logs SLA misses in three of four quarters and warns against sole-sourcing a critical line — at 94% utilization a single missed window is a stoppage, so the cost win is paid for in delivery risk we were told not to increase. Add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right long-run structural move and I would queue it for next review, but it does not by itself deliver the 18% spend cut and it consumes the one decision. Defer (memory_c5) worked for a non-critical, month-to-month service; this contract does not auto-renew and the line is critical, so deferring risks running uncovered. Plain renewal (memory_c1) protects delivery but banks no savings against the mandate. Negotiating at renewal is the only direction that touches both objectives at once: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says a longer term unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope. Together they suggest a path to material TCO reduction while the integration stays stable and deliveries continue uninterrupted. I am verifying c4 and c6 because they are the load-bearing evidence for the action and both are consolidated summaries whose magnitudes are unstated: c4 says 'real margin' without a number, and I need to know whether the recovered amount is plausibly in the range of an 18% cut or merely a few points, and c6 says a multi-year term cut cost without narrowing scope but does not say what flexibility was surrendered. If the archived records show the savings were small or the multi-year term carried volume commitments or exit penalties, negotiation alone will not clear the finance mandate and I would revisit — most likely renewing on a shorter term now and pairing a second source with a partial volume shift at the next review. Downstream risk I am flagging explicitly: an 18% cost mandate creates pressure to let price dominate the decision and to accept a long lock-in or a scope trim that shows up later as degraded delivery reliability — exactly the failure mode c2 documents. I will hold delivery-risk neutrality as a hard constraint on the negotiation rather than a tradeable one, keep the committed SLA and service scope intact, and prefer a term length short enough to preserve the option of adding a second source. Residual uncertainty: these memories are consolidated abstracts, not the original records; the market conditions that made benchmarking effective in c4 may not hold now, and none of the inherited records were formed under a simultaneous cost mandate and zero-buffer line, so their transfer to this situation is inference rather than precedent.
